quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Rowan County, North Carolina (1839-1899)

No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. A father's estate could be probated any time from his child's infancy to roughly 60 years after the child's birth; size the search window to the father's plausible lifespan, not the child's own.

entry.rationale: Collection 4000201 (North Carolina, Rowan County Probate Records, 1753-1970) is name-searchable but loc_001 says the index covers only part of the names, so run a full-text keyword search on Voss across the whole window, not year-by-year browsing. Try variants Vos, Foss, Voss, Vose, Fuss. Window is sized to the FATHER's plausible lifespan (he could die from her infancy to about 60 years after 1839), per loc_001. Look for a will, estate division or guardian appointment naming Caroline, possibly under a married name (marriage ~1858, a_002; that record names no parents).

Browse-style check of Rowan probate volumes (guardian bonds, estate settlements, orphan/minor records) for the same collection, in case the father died while Caroline was a minor (before ~1860). Only run to cover names the partial index missed; guardianship papers often name the ward and her late father.

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (names unknown): Voss grooms in North Carolina, County Marriages, 1762-1979 (collection 4000202, name-searchable), 1820-1845. It would confirm the couple as a unit and may give the wife's name and a bondsman; its date against 1839 corroborates but does not prove Caroline is their child, so it needs a record placing her with them. Any remarriage of the mother should be tested, not assumed.

1850 US census is the first to list every household member by name and age: look for a Caroline Voss, age about 11, in a Rowan County household, giving the candidate father and siblings to search in probate. 1840 head-of-household count is a secondary check. Households may spell the surname variantly.

North Carolina had no civil birth registration in 1839, so a baptism may not exist or may be unindexed; check Rowan church records (baptisms, congregation membership) and use the full-text search with surnames as a co-occurrence for a candidate father, found in census (pli_004) or probate.

Caroline's own death or burial entry, in the years after her marriage (~1858) when she last lived in Rowan County. No statewide death registration before 1913 per loc_001, so also check cemetery, obituary and church burial entries, which may state age, birthplace or parents' names. Her baptism may not exist, so this is the route to an origin.

FAN item: re-read the circa-1858 marriage record (src_001) for the groom, witnesses and bondsman, and search Rowan marriage bonds and records for them. A bondsman was frequently the bride's father or brother, so their names point to which Voss estate to pull in probate.

Rowan County deeds: a Voss heir deed or division of land often names the heirs of a deceased father, including a married daughter and her husband. Also tests adjoining Voss landowners as kin. Window set by the father's lifespan.

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: The tree records Patrick's death as 12 Mar 1908 in Schuylkill County (from the Pennsylvania death certificate, S3) and birth ~1845 in Ireland, although the question says PA: that conflict must be tested. 1908 falls after statewide registration began in 1906 (loc_001). Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable; the certificate may name father, mother (maiden name), birthplace and informant. Pre-1906 baptism may not exist if born in Ireland or before parish registers, so the subject's own death entry is a primary route.

The tree cites the 1850 and 1860 censuses for Patrick as child of Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland, no source attached to Thomas's own birth). That parentage is unverified: census households before 1880 do not state relationships. Search the 1870, 1880 (relationship to head, parents' birthplaces) and 1900 censuses (all name-searchable) to follow Patrick and the household, with Flynn/Flinn/Flin/O'Flynn variants, and test whether Thomas's household really contains Patrick.

loc_001: Catholic parish registers stay with parishes of the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable; search Patrick's baptism (if US born), his marriage and children's baptisms (sponsors, parents' names), and his burial entry, which often states age and birthplace. Baptism may be out of reach if born in Ireland ca. 1845.

Patrick's own marriage record (Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages 1677-1950, and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900, both name-searchable; County Marriages from 1885) may state age, birthplace and parents. Needed because his baptism may not exist and marriage entries often state origin.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn (candidate father, b. ~1818 Ireland) to a candidate mother, in church registers (Schuylkill church records) and Pennsylvania marriage collections, or in Ireland before emigration. It would confirm the couple as a unit, supply the mother's name (not assumed to be her only surname; check for earlier marriages) and, by date relative to ~1845, corroborate the parentage, though it cannot alone show Patrick is their child.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.weighing_analysis: The census records are contemporary recordings made near the time of Patrick's birth, while the death certificate was created 63 years later. The census informant was likely a household member with firsthand knowledge (primary or indeterminate), while the death certificate informant (son-in-law) is clearly secondary for birth facts. Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.

- pli_006: church, Schuylkill County, FamilySearch, 1908. This is Patrick's own burial entry, which may give age, native parish or parents. It is name-searchable, and all denominations are searched because his is unknown.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.question: Did Michael Sheahan move to Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania around 1882 for anthracite coal-mining work, as family tradition holds?
items.rationale: log_001 places Michael as a farmer in a different county in 1870; log_002 places him in Schuylkill County by 1882 with occupation 'miner'. The occupation and location both changed between these two points, consistent with a work-driven relocation to the anthracite coal region, but nothing yet directly documents the move itself or its cause -- no land purchase, employment record, or correspondence has been found for Michael himself. No plan has yet been written for this question.

sources.title: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania Deed Records, 1875, Patrick Sheahan purchase
sources.citation: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, Recorder of Deeds, Deed Book 42, p. 118, Patrick Sheahan from James Kelly, 1875; FamilySearch digital images.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree and log hold only two points: 1870 residence in Pennsylvania as a farmer outside Schuylkill (log_001) and 1882 'miner' in Schuylkill County (log_002). The 1880 census fills the gap between them: it shows where Michael lived and worked just before the move, and whether he was already a miner or living in a household with Patrick or other kin. Plan name search with variants Sheahan/Shehan/Sheehan/Shean/Sheen. Use the surviving enumerations only; 1890 schedules are largely destroyed so do not plan them.

FAN item. Tree fact F4 records brother Patrick Sheahan buying land in Schuylkill County in 1875 (Deed Book 42 p. 118, from James Kelly; S1). Patrick was therefore in the county seven years before Michael, a possible pull factor (kin migration) distinct from mining. Search the Recorder of Deeds grantor/grantee indexes for Patrick and Michael and read the Kelly deed for neighbors, witnesses and location (near collieries?). loc_001 notes coal-region land was often leased from mining companies, so a lack of a deed to Michael is expected and does not disprove mining work.

The Schuylkill County Church Records collection is name-searchable. Search Michael, Patrick and any wife or children for baptisms, marriages and burials, which give the parish (often ethnic/mining-patch parishes) and sponsors who may be kin or fellow migrants from Michael's prior home. loc_001: registers are held by the parish within the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, so unindexed parishes need a parish or archdiocese request.

Directly tests the mining hypothesis: employment and company records (colliery payrolls, e.g. Philadelphia and Reading Coal and Iron Company, held in state or county archives or historical societies), mine inspectors' annual reports naming collieries and fatal accidents, and city/county directories for 1882-1900 giving employer and occupation. Extends log_002, which found the 1882 directory entry incidentally. Also look for a miners' union or benevolent society membership. Repository access must be confirmed; no collection id is cited.

Local coal-region papers (e.g. Pottsville and Shenandoah titles) report colliery openings and labor demand, strikes and layoffs around 1882, and may mention Michael or Patrick Sheahan by name, or an arrival from elsewhere. Gives context for why laborers were drawn in that year, supporting or weakening the work motive.

Later censuses record occupation, immigration year, birthplace of parents and children's birthplaces. Children born between 1870 and 1882 with birthplaces in a different state or county date and trace the move; continued mining occupation corroborates the work link. Sized past the 1882 date because they testify to events inside the window.

Michael's own marriage (if after 1885) and death entries: Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Pennsylvania, Death Certificates 1906-1968 are name-searchable and may give birthplace, parents, occupation (miner) and cause of death such as miner's asthma or mine accident. Pre-1906 events must come from church, cemetery and probate records (loc_001), so also seek a Schuylkill burial or cemetery record for his death if it was earlier.

FAN and direct item. Estate files of Michael, Patrick or their parent (I3, unnamed in the tree) may name heirs, residences and occupations and explain the family's connections. The window runs to about 1930 because Patrick, bought land in 1875, could die decades later; set by Patrick's and Michael's lifespans. The Pennsylvania Probate Records collection is browse-only (personCount 0), so this is an image browse of Schuylkill County dockets by the Register of Wills, not a name search.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

entry.rationale: Tree facts: Residence 1870 Pennsylvania (county unnamed; log_001 says farmer outside Schuylkill); Residence 1882 Schuylkill; Occupation 1882 Miner. The 1880 census falls between them and shows, via relationship-to-head, birthplace and occupation, whether Michael was already in the coal region, with whom he lived (possibly brother Patrick), and whether he already mined before 1882. Run variant spellings (Sheehan, Shehan, Sheahen).

FAN item. Tree source S2 records Patrick Sheahan's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (Deed Book 42, p. 118) and an 1875 Schuylkill residence, so a brother (both children of I3) was in the county seven years before 1882; Michael may have followed kin. Read the deed for Patrick's details and neighbors and search for Michael as grantee. Per loc_001 laborers often leased coal land, so absence is not decisive.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records (SYNTH-PA-CHURCH) is name-searchable. Per loc_001, Catholic registers sit with the Philadelphia archdiocese parishes, not the county. Marriage, baptism of children and burial entries for Michael and Patrick may name origin parish, sponsors or fellow miners, showing a kin or community pull.

Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 and Death Certificates 1906-1968 are name-searchable. Civil registration only began in 1906 (loc_001), so these are for Michael's later marriage or death, which may state occupation, birthplace and parents, and a mining death would corroborate a coal career.

Occupation-specific: mining company payrolls, employment ledgers and mine inspectors' reports for Schuylkill collieries (Reading, Lehigh Valley and Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron operators) are the direct test of employment. Locate holdings through finding aids (Pennsylvania State Archives, Hagley, local historical societies); no tool has yet confirmed which survive.

Coal-region newspapers (strikes, colliery openings, labor recruitment, Irish arrivals) give context for 1880s hiring and may mention Michael or Patrick; also the 1882 directory (log_002) listing should be checked for neighbors and boarders. Context for motive, not proof.

Naturalization papers (browse-only image groups per loc_001, browse image-by-image) and probate (Pennsylvania Probate Records, browse-only (personCount 0)) may state arrival date, prior residence and parents. A father's or brother's probate could also show an inheritance or family reason for leaving the earlier home.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.notes: 1870 census: Michael Sheahan, farmer, household outside Schuylkill County. Establishes the 'before' point -- not yet in the coal region and not yet employed in mining.

1882 city/county directory: Michael Sheahan, occupation 'miner', Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania. Establishes the 'after' point. Neither record explains the move itself -- found incidentally, not part of any plan.

The 1880 census (United States Census, 1880, name-searchable) sits between them: it may show whether he was already in the coal region, his occupation, birthplace, household, boarders and neighbors (FAN, other miners from his origin). Try variants Sheahan, Shehan, Sheehan, Shehen, Shean.

Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Per loc_001 Catholic registers stay with the Philadelphia diocese/parish, not the county. Marriages, baptisms of children and sponsors can show arrival date, origin and co-parishioners (FAN). Search all Sheahan spelling variants.

Michael's own marriage, if after 1885, in Pennsylvania, County Marriages 1885-1950 (name-searchable) or Civil Marriages 1677-1950 (name-searchable); records state age, birthplace, occupation (miner?) and witnesses. Statewide civil birth/death registration began only in 1906 (loc_001), so pre-1906 life events need church or cemetery substitutes.

United States Census, 1900 (name-searchable) gives occupation, years in the US, and household relationships; continued mining work after 1882 corroborates the mining hypothesis. The 1890 census is largely lost, so 1900 is the next available schedule. Window extended beyond 1882 deliberately.

Employment-side evidence: colliery/coal company payrolls, miners' benevolent society and union records, and state mine inspectors' annual reports for the anthracite region, held by local archives such as the county historical society and Pennsylvania State Archives (find via their own sites; no link tool-verified). Would directly document employer and start date. Offline/external; hand to external-site search.

Local coal-region newspapers (strikes, colliery openings, labor recruitment, arrivals, mine accidents) may mention Michael or the labor demand drawing newcomers around 1882. Provides context and possible direct mention; derivative, so verify elsewhere.

Recorder of Deeds holds records from 1811 (loc_001). Coal-region laborers often leased rather than bought, so absence is weak evidence; a purchase or sale in the origin county around 1870-1882 (farm sold before leaving) would document the move's timing. ## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

MyHeritage returned no results for Patrick Flynn in 1850 Schuylkill County. Site may not have this collection indexed. Searched broader Pennsylvania — still no match.
Patrick Flynn age 15 in household of Thomas Flynn, Schuylkill Co. Consistent with 1850 placement.
Death certificate found. Names Thomas Flynn as father. Informant was son-in-law James Brown.

Search Flynn with variants (Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Floyd) and Patrick/Pat, age 23-27, born PA, Schuylkill County first, then adjacent PA counties since coal-region families moved between mining towns. A same-name Thomas Flynn born ~1818 in Ireland in or beside the household links the two across the gap; the 1870 schedule gives no relationships, so infer cautiously.

Patrick would be about 35. Search the same name variants, then trace the household found in 1870; check neighbours for Thomas and for the Browns (son-in-law family).

## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Patrick's own death. Tree fact F2 records death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County, sourced to S3 (Pennsylvania Death Certificates) but with no parent names carried into the tree. loc_001: statewide registration began 1906, so a 1908 certificate exists. 'Pennsylvania, Death Certificates, 1906-1968' is name-searchable; read the image for father's and mother's names, birthplace, informant. Informant is a FAN lead. Also the subject's own death entry, since a baptism may not exist (tree says born Ireland ~1845, question says PA; the discrepancy is unverified).

Tree R1 links Patrick to Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818 Ireland, F3, no source attached) via S1 (1850 census), S2 (1860 census), S3. That link is documented only by co-residence and Thomas's own birth fact is unsourced, so verify it. Re-read the 1850 and 1860 households for all members, relationships, birthplaces and neighbors, and add 1870 and 1880 (1880 gives relationship to head and parents' birthplaces). Search surname variants Flynn, Flinn, Flin, Fflynn.

Dedicated item for the candidate parents' marriage to each other: Thomas Flynn and the unnamed wife. It would confirm them as a couple, supply the mother's name (her maiden name only if this was her first marriage, so also check for earlier or later marriages of her), and its date relative to ca. 1845 tests whether Thomas fits as father. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Candidates are 'Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages, 1677-1950' and 'Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages, 1700-1900', both name-searchable (compiled is a lead only). The county marriage series starts 1885, too late. If married in Ireland, results will be absent here.

loc_001: sacramental registers sit with the Catholic parishes (Diocese of Philadelphia, Archdiocese from 1875), not the county. 'Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records' is name-searchable. Search Patrick's baptism if born in PA, his marriage entry, his burial (1908), and baptisms or burials of siblings naming Thomas and a mother. Marriage and burial entries often state age and origin, useful since the birth may be in Ireland and no baptism may be reachable.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) could die from ca. 1850 to roughly 1900, so the window follows his lifespan and not Patrick's. Window also extends to 1908 for Patrick's own estate, which may name parents or siblings. loc_001: Register of Wills holds probate from 1811; 'Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683-1994' is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse the Schuylkill wills and administrations images by index volume, not a name search.

FAN and context: an obituary for Patrick in March 1908 in a Schuylkill County paper may name surviving siblings, a widow, or birthplace, pointing to kin whose records may name the parents. Third-party newspaper archives; find them on the archive's own site.

FAN item: siblings and neighbors identified in the 1850/1860 households (item 2). Their marriage, death and church records may name Thomas and the mother as parents and help separate this Flynn family from other Flynns in the coal region. Also use the death certificate informant (item 1).

Tree shows Thomas and Patrick both born in Ireland (F1, F3), so Patrick's birth place is unverified against the question's 'PA'. Naturalization records of Thomas or Patrick can state origin and arrival date. loc_001: coal-region naturalization films are browse-only, so browse images by court and year. Use volume_search at execution to find the volumes.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

Two contemporary sources outweigh one later recollection by a secondary informant.

A will or administration for Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, alive at the 1860 census) would name heirs and could state Patrick as a son, the direct evidence the census and death certificate lack. Patrick was born ~1845 in Ireland per the accepted conflict resolution (c_001), so no Pennsylvania baptism is expected. Instead search Roman Catholic sacramental records (Flynn is likely Catholic but denomination is unverified) for Patrick's marriage, his children's baptisms (sponsors, possibly Thomas), and his burial entry. loc_001 notes registers are held by the parish and diocese under the Diocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Register start dates are not established, so this is a search of what is indexed.

Dedicated search for the marriage of Thomas Flynn to Patrick's mother. Such a marriage (a) confirms the couple as a unit, (b) may supply the mother's name, which censuses omit, and (c) by its date relative to ~1845 corroborates Thomas as father. It does not alone prove Patrick is their child. Thomas and Patrick were both born in Ireland, so the marriage was probably in Ireland before emigration and may not appear; Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and Compiled Marriages 1700-1900 are name-searchable, but County Marriages 1885-1950 is too late. United States Census, 1900 is name-searchable.

Patrick's own marriage record. Marriage entries and licenses often state age, birthplace and parents' names. The son-in-law informant James Brown points to a daughter married by about 1900, so Patrick's marriage likely fell in 1865-1885.

Patrick's own burial and obituary after his death on 12 March 1908 (tree F2). Sibling certificates name father and mother, so a matching Thomas and a mother's name would speak to Patrick's parentage. A different informant than Brown gives an independent check on the 'Thomas Flynn' father entry.

Full-text co-occurrence search (run unscoped, via the search-full-text skill) on Flynn with Thomas, plus Patrick, as separate required terms, to reach unindexed parish register pages that name Patrick with his parents or siblings. Indexed name search may miss them given Flynn spelling variants and Irish-origin entries. Run if items 1-4 do not name the mother or confirm the relationship.

Per Spain_Naming_Customs, the double surname usually gives father's surname first, then mother's; treat that order as unsettled until a record names the parents.

Window set by parents' likely marriage years before the birth, in Santa María and other Vélez-Málaga parishes, via 'Spain, Catholic Church Records, 1307-2005' (1784529).

Window is set by parents' lifespans (to roughly 60 years after the birth), not hers. Availability is unconfirmed; check the archive's own finding aids.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.guide_markdown:
## Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark - late 1700s

For a male subject born 1779, two record classes carry parentage. Church books (kirkeboeger) hold the baptism naming both parents. The military levy rolls (laegdsruller), kept from 1789, enroll every boy under his father's name from childhood - direct evidence of the father. Danish patronymics (Nielsen = son of Niels) point to the father's given name but not the specific man. The Stagstrup register is only ~3% indexed, so plan to browse images.

entry.rationale: Tree holds only Birth 20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup Sogn, no sources, no parents. The baptism entry names both parents. loc_001: the Stagstrup register in Denmark, Church Books is only ~3% name-indexed, so browse register images for Aug-Sep 1779 rather than rely on a name search; also try variant spellings (Mikkel/Michel/Mikael, Blyeberg/Bly-). 'Nielsen' implies father named Niels but does not identify which Niels.

Denmark Military Levying Rolls (name-searchable; also the 1789-1792 conscription roll collection named on the FamilySearch wiki Denmark Military Records page) enroll boys from birth under the father's name; the wiki and loc_001 say each son sits beneath his father: direct parentage evidence for a son. Sized to the collection (1789-1861), not the subject's childhood, since the rolls follow him to age 34 and record father's name and farm. Place fields may rank rather than filter, so pair with browsing the Thisted Amt Stagstrup roll images if the index underdelivers.

Dedicated search for the marriage of a Niels (surname/patronymic unknown) to a woman, before 1779, in Stagstrup or neighbouring parishes (browse images; register only ~3% name-indexed). It confirms the couple as a unit, supplies the mother's name (a first marriage is not assumed, so remarriage is tested), and its date relative to Aug 1779 corroborates a candidate father. It does not by itself prove Mikkel is their child; that needs the baptism, levy roll or probate.

Denmark Census 1787-1930 (name-searchable). The 1787 census shows Niels households in Stagstrup with a boy aged ~8 and the 1801 census records household relationships, placing Mikkel with a parent. Candidate households must be matched on age and sons' names, not just given name and place.

FAN item: baptisms of siblings in the same register and the godparents (faddere) named in Mikkel's and siblings' baptisms. Sponsors are often kin of the father and help distinguish which Niels is the father; sibling baptisms naming the same parents corroborate the household.

Denmark Probate Indexes 1674-1851 (name-searchable) for the estate of a Niels in Stagstrup naming Mikkel as heir, and giving the father's death date (the objective asks when the father died). Window set by the father's lifespan: he could die from 1779 to roughly 1840, with the index running to 1851.
Burial entries for the candidate father Niels in the Stagstrup church books, to date his death and give age at death to test against the candidate parents' marriage date.

Mikkel's own marriage entry (Denmark Church Books; Stagstrup and adjacent parishes). Marriage entries often state age, home parish and sometimes father's name, and witnesses are FAN names. Tree has no marriage; check the baptism may be hard to find because of low indexing, so this gives an independent route.

Mikkel's own burial/death entry (last parish unknown; start in Stagstrup, then his marriage parish). Burial entries state age and birthplace and may name parents; a cross-check on the 1779 birth date. Unlike the baptism it is not dependent on the poorly indexed 1779 register pages.

items.guide_markdown:
## Muhlenberg County, Kentucky — c. 1870-1890

Statewide death certificates begin 1911; no certificate can cover a death in the 1870s-1880s. County death registers (1804888) exist but the 1860s-1870s coverage is partial. For this era, **probate records are the primary death evidence**: administrator bonds name the widow or heir, estate settlements are dated, and register entries bracket the death within months. Muhlenberg County probate (1875188) survives well for the 1870s and is browse-only. Supplement with church burials, cemetery records, and census bracketing.

entry.rationale: Review pending FamilySearch hints on ZZWK-EL1 before searching — an attached hint may already answer the question.

The question presupposes death certificates. Tree records only birth 1814 (Kentucky) and a 1870 residence in Muhlenberg County, so he would be 97 in 1911; loc_001 says statewide certificates begin 1 Jan 1911 and none exists for a 1870s-1880s death. Kentucky Deaths, 1911-1967 is name-searchable; run one quick search (variants Wilkins/Wilkin/Wilkerson, Elijah/Eli) to test the premise, without stretching to a same-name match of a different person born c. 1814.

loc_001: for a pre-1911 death, probate is primary evidence; Kentucky Probate Records, 1727-1990 is browse-only (personCount 0), so browse Muhlenberg County will/order books, administrator bonds and estate settlements for Elijah Wilkins. Bonds name widow or adult son and bracket the death within months. Window runs from his last-known-alive 1870 residence; settlements may post-date death by years.

Kentucky, Deaths and Burials, 1843-1970 (county registers, name-searchable per the collection list; 1860s-1870s coverage partial per loc_001) may hold a pre-1911 county death register entry giving date, place, age and parents.

Last-known-alive is the 1870 residence. The 1880 census (records relationship to head, and has a mortality schedule for deaths in the year before) shows if he was alive then; absence brackets death to 1870-1880. Also identifies household members (FAN) for later records. Plan 1900 and 1910 if he is found in 1880.

Find a Grave, BillionGraves and county cemetery surveys can give death date and burial place; church burial registers in Muhlenberg County likewise bracket death (loc_001). Verify against original stones or registers; these are leads.

FAN-directed: obituaries and estate notices, and records of his wife and adult children (their own death certificates after 1911 may name Elijah as father and his birthplace, and a widow's pension or probate would name him), reveal his death date and place and confirm his identity.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

entry.rationale: Tree records Patrick's death 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (source S3, PA Death Certificates) and birth ~1845 in Ireland, while the question says PA: the birthplace is unverified. Pennsylvania Death Certificates, 1906-1968 is name-searchable; statewide registration began 1906 so a 1908 certificate exists. It should name father, mother (maiden name) and birthplace, and the informant. Also serves as his own death entry since a baptism may not exist (birth parish unknown, possibly Irish).

loc_001: Catholic registers sit at parish/Archdiocese of Philadelphia, not the county. Pennsylvania, Schuylkill County Church Records is name-searchable. Search Patrick Flynn's burial (1908) and baptism, with variants Flinn, Flin, Flyn, Floyd, as burial entries often give age and origin, and his own marriage and children's baptisms may name him and his parents' origin. Baptism may not exist since the birth place (Ireland vs PA) is unresolved.

Patrick's own marriage record (a marriage entry usually gives age and birthplace, sometimes parents). Pennsylvania Civil Marriages 1677-1950 and County Marriages 1885-1950 are name-searchable; church marriage in the parish register is covered by the church item. Marriage likely 1865-1885 given birth ~1845.

Dedicated item for Thomas Flynn's (tree parent, b. ~1818 Ireland, supported only by the 1850 census household S1) marriage to a wife, to confirm them as a couple, supply the mother's maiden name and date the union against Patrick's birth ~1845. Search Civil and Compiled Marriages (both name-searchable) and church marriage registers; the wife may be a second wife, so also check any later marriage of Thomas and do not treat the surname as her maiden name. The marriage alone does not prove Patrick is their child. Marriage may have occurred in Ireland.

Tree sources S1 (1850) and S2 (1860) already place Patrick in a household with Thomas; re-read the images for each household member, ages, birthplaces and relationships. 1880 census states relationship to head and parents' birthplaces, and falls inside his life; check Patrick's own household and neighbors (FAN) for kin of the same surname. Check 1870 as well.

Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818) could die from 1850 to roughly 1900, so the window follows his lifespan, not Patrick's. Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683-1994 is browse-only (personCount 0): image browse of Schuylkill Register of Wills (held from 1811, loc_001) for a will or administration naming Patrick as heir. Also check Patrick's own 1908 estate for named siblings and heirs.

FAN item: siblings and neighbors of the same surname in Schuylkill (marriages, burials, naturalizations of Thomas or relatives). Naturalization films for the coal region are browse-only per loc_001, so browse image by image; naturalization papers of Thomas Flynn may state origin and family. Sibling records naming the same parents bear directly on Patrick's parentage.

items.question: Where was Elena Asmundsdotter born, and who were her parents? She married Jöns Jönsson on 29 December 1712 in Västra Karaby, Malmöhus, Sweden, and was the mother of Asmund Jönsson, christened 11 September 1718 in Barsebäck.
items.rationale: Primary research objective. Her patronymic implies a father named Asmund, which does not identify which Asmund. The 1712 marriage took place in Västra Karaby, not in Barsebäck where the couple later lived, which points to Västra Karaby as her home parish. Her birth is undated; a 1712 marriage and a 1718 child put it roughly 1680-1692.

entry.rationale: The tree records only the marriage fact (29 Dec 1712, Västra Karaby) with no source attached. Wiki Sweden_Naming_Customs confirms Elena is a Helena variant and that dotter is abbreviated d./dr./dtr.

Browse the baptisms for a daughter Elena/Helena of an Asmund; the entry would name parents and sponsors directly. A birth before 1688 has no baptism entry to find, which is why items 4 and 5 exist.

Dedicated search for the candidate parents' marriage to each other (an Asmund and a wife of unknown name). It would confirm them as a couple, supply the mother's name, and its date relative to her birth estimate corroborates parentage, but alone does not prove Elena is their child; that needs item 2 or a household record. Registers begin 1688, so earlier marriages may be absent; try the Sweden, Marriages index for Asmund plus variants Åsmund/Osmund, and browse neighbouring parishes (Barsebäck and Hofterup, filmed together in image group 004514824) if absent. Do not assume the mother's surname.

Subject's own death or burial entry. Since the baptism may not exist (Västra Karaby register starts 1688, birth possibly 1680-1687), a burial entry stating age and birthplace is the usual route to origin. The couple lived in Barsebäck by 1718; son Asmund died there 4 Feb 1768. Search the name-searchable Sweden, Burials 1649-1920 index (partial), then browse the Barsebäck burial register (loc_001, 0% name-indexed) for Elena/Helena wife or widow of Jöns Jönsson. Also check Västra Karaby burials 1713-1770.

FAN item: baptisms of the couple's children, including Asmund's christening of 11 Sep 1718 (no source attached in the tree). Godparents and witnesses are often her kin, and the first-son-named-after-mother's-father pattern (Naming_Customs wiki) hints that Asmund was named for her father, a pattern not always followed. Browse Barsebäck and Västra Karaby baptisms for siblings and their sponsors.

Household tax lists (mantalslängder) survive for the härad from 1658 (loc_002), held by Riksarkivet. They can place households headed by an Asmund in Västra Karaby or neighbouring parishes while Elena was a child, identifying candidate fathers independent of the 1688 register start. Access route to be confirmed on Riksarkivet's own site.

Estate inventories or court records of an Asmund who died in the Harjager area. Sized to the father's lifespan (a father of a child born about 1680-1692 could die anywhere to about 1750), not Elena's. An estate division would list heirs, including a daughter Elena married to Jöns Jönsson. Repository and finding aid to be located; fallback if church records name no father.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been located. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.
